result: Hsp47 directly interacts with GABAA receptor subunits with high affinity in multiple experimental contexts.
evaluation: Claims C41-C43 demonstrate direct binding in mouse brain, in vitro, and in cells through co-immunoprecipitation and pulldown assays (Figure 1A-B). Claims C47-C49 provide quantitative binding affinity measurements (Kd ~100-127 nM) via MST (Figure 1C). The convergence of multiple independent binding assays across different experimental systems strongly supports direct, high-affinity interaction.

result: Hsp47 positively regulates functional surface expression of endogenous GABAA receptors in neurons.
evaluation: Claims C52-C54 show knockdown decreases surface staining of α1, β2/3, and γ2 subunits (Figure 2A), while C55-C57 show overexpression increases surface staining (Figure 2B). Claims C58-C59 provide functional validation through electrophysiology showing decreased currents with knockdown (1660→886 pA) and increased currents with overexpression (→2455 pA) (Figure 2C). The combination of immunofluorescence and functional data provides strong support.

result: Hsp47 preferentially binds folded GABAA receptor conformations and acts after BiP in the biogenesis pathway.
evaluation: Claims C71-C72 show DTT treatment (disrupting disulfide bonds) decreases Hsp47-α1 interaction (Figure 3B). Claims C73-C74 show genetic disruption of disulfide bonds (C166A mutations) similarly decreases Hsp47 binding (Figure 3C). Conversely, claims C81-C83 show the same treatments increase BiP binding (Figure 3E-F), demonstrating opposite binding preferences. Claims C75-C77 show misfolded variants aggregate more (Figure 3D). This comprehensive dataset strongly supports sequential action and conformational preference.

result: Hsp47 promotes GABAA receptor subunit assembly and ER-to-Golgi trafficking.
evaluation: Claims C86-C87 show Hsp47 overexpression increases FRET efficiency between α1-CFP and β2-YFP (24.4%→31.7%) (Figure 4A). Claim C88 shows increased co-immunoprecipitation of β2 with α1 (Figure 4B). Claims C94-C95 show increased 480 kDa oligomeric complex formation on non-reducing gels (Figure 4C-D). Claims C60-C62 show increased Endo H resistance indicating enhanced ER-to-Golgi trafficking (Figure 3A). Multiple orthogonal assays converge on the same conclusion.

result: Hsp47 overexpression rescues surface expression and function of epilepsy-associated GABAA receptor variants.
evaluation: Claims C102-C104 show Hsp47 increases Endo H resistance for α1(A322D) variant (0.20→0.35 ratio) (Figure 5A). Claims C110-C111 show increased surface and total protein levels (Figure 5C). Claim C112 shows functional rescue with increased GABA-induced currents (8.5→50.3 pA) (Figure 5D). Claims C113-C118 demonstrate similar rescue for three additional variants (S76R, D219N, G251D) with 1.59-1.87-fold current increases (Figure 5F-G). The consistency across multiple disease variants strongly supports therapeutic potential.

result: Hsp47 manipulation does not activate the unfolded protein response (UPR).
evaluation: Claims C120-C125 show knockdown/overexpression of Hsp47 does not change XBP1s, ATF6-N, or CHOP levels in HEK293T cells (Figure 6A-B), while C126 shows thapsigargin (positive control) does increase these markers. Claim C129 shows similar results in neurons (Figure 6C). Claims C131-C133 show UPR activation does not increase Hsp47 levels (Figure 6D). The bidirectional experiments with appropriate controls strongly support independence from global UPR.

result: Hsp47 has a general role in promoting surface expression of heteropentameric Cys-loop receptors.
evaluation: Claims C136-C138 show Hsp47 increases α4β2 nAChR protein levels and FRET efficiency (27.7%→40.9%) (Figure 7A-B). Claim C142 shows increased nicotine-induced currents (57.9→134 pA) (Figure 7C). Claims C144-C145 show increased surface expression of 5-HT3A/B subunits (Figure 7D). The demonstration of similar effects across three different Cys-loop receptor families (GABAA, nAChR, 5-HT3R) strongly supports generality.

result: Hsp47 shows selectivity for heteropentameric Cys-loop receptors and does not affect other ion channels or ERAD substrates.
evaluation: Claims C139-C140 show no effect on homopentameric α7 nAChRs (Figure 7—supplement 1A-B). Claims C147-C149 show no positive effect on NMDA receptors (Figure 7—supplement 2A). Claims C150-C152 show no effect on hERG channels (Figure 7—supplement 2B). Claims C153-C154 show no effect on L444P β-glucocerebrosidase (Figure 7—supplement 2C). The systematic testing of structurally diverse controls demonstrates specificity, though the negative results rely on absence of effect.

result: Hsp47 plays a critical and general role in multi-subunit Cys-loop receptor maturation through direct effects on assembly.
evaluation: This integrative claim is supported by the convergence of multiple result groups: direct binding (C41-C49), preferential binding to folded states (C71-C84), promotion of assembly (C86-C95), rescue of disease variants (C102-C118), effects on multiple receptor types (C136-C145), and independence from UPR (C120-C135). The mechanistic model is well-supported by diverse experimental approaches, though some details about assembly intermediates remain to be determined.

result: Background claims about molecular chaperones, GABAA receptors, and Hsp47 from prior literature.
evaluation: These claims (C16-C40) establish the scientific context through citations to prior work. They describe established knowledge about chaperone function, GABAA receptor structure/function, disease associations, and Hsp47's known roles. All claims are appropriately cited and represent accurate summaries of prior literature. These provide essential background but are not novel findings of this study.

result: Hsp47 shows selectivity in binding membrane proteins and is co-distributed with GABAA receptors in brain regions.
evaluation: Claims C44-C45 show Hsp47 does not bind hERG or ZIP7 in vitro (Figure 1—supplement 2A), supporting C46's inference of selectivity. Claims C50-C51 show co-distribution of Hsp47 and GABAA receptors in multiple brain regions (Figure 2—supplement 1A). These provide supporting evidence for specificity and physiological relevance, though the in vitro selectivity data has limitations regarding protein folding states.

result: Hsp47 increases total protein levels and trafficking efficiency without changing degradation rates.
evaluation: Claims C161-C164 show Hsp47 increases total protein and ER-to-Golgi trafficking for both WT and A322D variants (Figures 4C, 5C, 3A, 5A). Claims C66-C67 and C107-C108 show no change in degradation rates via cycloheximide-chase (Figure 3—supplement 1C-D, Figure 5—supplement 1A-B). Claims C64-C65 show decreased ubiquitination (Figure 3—supplement 1B, 5B). This supports the model that Hsp47 shifts receptor populations toward trafficking-competent states rather than affecting degradation.

result: Discussion claims about BiP function, receptor assembly mechanisms, Hsp47's known substrates, and therapeutic implications.
evaluation: These claims (C79-C80, C157, C176-C192) provide mechanistic context and discuss implications. Claims about BiP (C79-C80) and assembly domains (C176-C177) cite prior work. Claims about Hsp47's substrate diversity (C178-C185) integrate prior knowledge with current findings. Claims about therapeutic potential (C188-C192) are supported by the rescue data (Figure 5) and prior citations. These represent appropriate interpretation and contextualization of the results.

result: Control experiments showing Hsp47 effects are specific to assembled receptors and more dramatic for disease variants.
evaluation: Claims C97-C98 show Hsp47 overexpression does not affect α1 monomers that cannot exit the ER (Figure 4C, lanes 12-15, 17-20), demonstrating specificity for assembled complexes. Claim C119 notes greater rescue effects for trafficking-deficient variants versus WT receptors (comparing Figures 3—supplement 1A, 5D, 5G). These controls strengthen the main conclusions by demonstrating specificity and suggesting therapeutic selectivity.
